waypoints.name: Rainy Pass PCT North Trailhead
waypoints.note: SR-20 milepost ~159, ~2 mi east of Rainy Pass; NPS backcountry permit required for overnight camping, $5/day USFS parking fee, no potable water on site.
waypoints.directions: Park at the Rainy Pass PCT North trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 159, about two miles east of Rainy Pass. A $5-per-day USFS parking fee applies here, and there's no potable water on site. An NPS backcountry permit is required for overnight camping in the Goode Glacier/moraine camp zone; reserve it in advance at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.

waypoints.name: PCT / North Fork Bridge Creek Trail junction
waypoints.note: Leave the Pacific Crest Trail here and turn onto the North Fork Bridge Creek Trail toward Goode's north side.

waypoints.name: Grizzly Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Usually an easy log crossing but reported as a dangerously high, hard-to-find ford in early season; trail turns brushy/overgrown just beyond it.

waypoints.name: Lateral moraine camp above Goode Glacier
waypoints.note: Established bivy atop the lateral moraine overlooking the Goode Glacier's seracs; standard base camp for the Southwest Couloir attempt.

waypoints.name: Goode Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Cross the glacier from the moraine camp to reach the couloir base; route-finding is tricky and late-season snow bridges can be deteriorated.

waypoints.name: Black Tooth Notch
waypoints.note: Foot-wide notch gained by an exposed class 4 traverse (fixed sling marks the crux step); rock here is loose/"garbage" — watch for rockfall onto climbers below.

waypoints.name: Goode Mountain summit
waypoints.note: Highest point in North Cascades National Park; summit block above the notch adds exposed class 4-5 moves before the true top.

weather.typical: Drier east-side (rain-shadow) climate than the west Cascades; midsummer is the stable window, spring carries lingering snow/avalanche risk on approach slopes and winter brings full snow cover

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Moderate: loose scree and talus on the south slopes create rockfall and twisted-ankle/fall risk typical of Class 2-3 terrain rather than sheer exposure; the primary hazard is the remoteness of the long, committing approach itself, which raises the consequence of any injury

fitnessSpec.hiking: ~11-13 miles round trip with roughly 4,900 ft of gain via the Nason Ridge trail and meadows; a long full day on the ridge
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Standard day-scramble pack (~15-20 lb: water, layers, navigation, basic first aid) - no technical rack needed for this route

partner_requirements.approachTime: ~5 hours to the summit from the Merritt Lake trailhead (per on-the-ground trip reports), longer if combined with Mount Howard
requiredSkills: off-trail routefinding through heather and talus (trail thins above treeline)
steady footing on loose scree and steep heather slopes
basic exposure tolerance for narrow ridge sections
map/GPS navigation - route is not signed or continuously trailed
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Intermediate scrambler - comfortable with off-trail routefinding, loose talus, and short exposed Class 3 ridge moves; not a beginner hike despite the Class 2-3 grade
